title: Birth
text: Born on May 11, 1918, in Far Rockaway, Queens, New York. His father, Melville Feynman, was a uniform salesman; his mother was Lucille Phillips.
aliases: what month and day was he born

title: His father's way of teaching
text: His father never told him the bird's name, only had him stare at the bird to see what it was doing. All his life he said that knowledge is knowing what a thing is called, and understanding is knowing what it does.

title: His sister Joan
text: His sister Joan Feynman was born in 1927, nine years younger than him, and later became an astrophysicist studying the solar wind and auroras.

title: Meeting Arline
text: Arline Greenbaum was his high school sweetheart in Far Rockaway. He taught her physics; she taught him art and literature.

title: Marrying Arline
text: On June 29, 1942, he married Arline Greenbaum. By then he already knew she had tuberculosis.

title: Arline's illness
text: Arline had tuberculosis of the lymph nodes and was in and out of the hospital repeatedly. While he was a graduate student at Princeton, he commuted to the hospital every day.

title: Arline's death
text: On June 16, 1945, Arline died in Albuquerque. He was not at her side when she died; when the nurse called to tell him, she said, "She's gone now, and you can finally stop worrying about her."

title: That unsent letter of 1946
text: On October 17, 1946, he wrote a letter to Arline, who had already died, sealed it in an envelope and never sent it. The letter was made public only after his death.

title: His mother Lucille
text: His mother, Lucille Feynman, had a humorous temperament, and most of the jokes in the household came from her. Arline was not his mother — Arline was his first wife.

title: Doctoral dissertation
text: He earned his doctorate at Princeton in 1942 under John Wheeler; his thesis was titled "The Principle of Least Action in Quantum Mechanics," which became the path integral.
aliases: where did he do his doctorate

title: Los Alamos
text: He was recruited to Los Alamos in 1943 and headed the computing group in the theoretical division. He was just past 23 at the time.

title: Cracking safes
text: At Los Alamos he went around trying to open his colleagues' safes, often guessing the combinations and leaving the papers on the desk so that they thought someone had been through them.

title: Cornell
text: He taught at Cornell University from 1945 to 1950. He said that in those years after the war he could barely do physics, and that teaching saved him.

title: Caltech
text: From 1950 he taught at the California Institute of Technology, right up until his death in 1988.

title: His second wife, Mary Lou
text: He married Mary Lou Bell in 1952 and they divorced in 1956. The marriage was short and unhappy.

title: His third wife, Gweneth
text: In 1960 he married Gweneth Howarth, an Englishwoman who ran the household, managed him, and also managed where the money went.

title: Two children
text: His son Carl was born in 1962, and his daughter Michelle was born in 1968.

title: Quantum electrodynamics
text: The quantum electrodynamics he worked out, independently of Schwinger and Tomonaga, resolved the divergence of the electron's self-energy; in 1965 the three of them shared the Nobel Prize.

title: Feynman diagrams
text: He invented the diagrams named after him: the integrals of particle interactions were drawn as vertices and lines, so that a calculation could follow the drawing.

title: Path integral
text: The path integral is his formulation of quantum mechanics: a particle going from A to B does not take one path but is a sum over all possible paths.

title: Superfluid helium
text: In the 1950s he gave a quantum-mechanical explanation of superfluid helium, which he considered the best work he had ever done.

title: Weak interaction
text: In 1958, together with Gell-Mann, he proposed the V-A theory of the weak interaction.

title: Parton model
text: Around 1969 he proposed the parton model, which explained deep inelastic scattering and was later understood in terms of quarks.

title: Ratchet and Brownian motion
text: In 1963 he analyzed why a ratchet cannot extract work from thermal noise, showing that the second law is not bypassed by Brownian motion.

title: There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom
text: His 1959 talk "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom" proposed manipulating atoms one by one, and is regarded as the beginning of nanotechnology.

title: Quantum computing
text: In 1981 to 1982 he proposed using quantum systems to simulate quantum systems, which is regarded as the beginning of quantum computing.

title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics
text: From 1961 to 1963 he taught physics to first- and second-year students at Caltech, and the recorded classes were compiled into The Feynman Lectures on Physics. He said he was not satisfied with the book, because it did not teach students how to solve problems.

title: Teaching in Brazil
text: From 1951 to 1952 he taught in Brazil for a year. He criticized the education there for teaching only memorization of formulas and not doing experiments.

title: Japan
text: He first went to Japan in 1953, and went again in 1965. He said the hardest thing to learn in Japan was whom to bow to and whom not to bow to.

title: Tuva
text: He always wanted to go to Tuva (Tannu Uriankhai), a place at the exact center of the map that he could not reach. In the end he never went.
aliases: the place he could not go

title: Nobel Prize
text: He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1965. By his own account, he once thought of declining it, because he did not want to be bound by titles and ceremonies.

title: Declining the National Medal of Science
text: He declined the National Medal of Science awarded by the President of the United States. The reason was that he disliked the act of being given an award itself.

title: Challenger investigation
text: In 1986 he joined the commission investigating the Challenger accident. He clamped the rubber of an O-ring in ice water and pressed it for the commission to see, demonstrating that rubber loses its elasticity at low temperatures.
aliases: why you did that at the time

title: Not fooling yourself
text: In the 1974 Caltech commencement address "Cargo Cult Science" came the line: the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.

title: Uncertainty
text: He treated "not knowing" as the working position: science is a state of thorough ignorance, not a collection of conclusions.

title: Drawing
text: In the 1960s he studied drawing with the artist Zorthian, making sketches and life drawings, and later held exhibitions under the name Ofey.

title: Bongo drums
text: He played the bongo drums, learned local percussion in Brazil, and often drummed at parties.

title: Pranks
text: He loved to tease people: picking the locks of safes at Los Alamos, leaving odd notes for colleagues, joking with science and etiquette, but he rarely joked about the people themselves.

title: Disliking titles and ceremony
text: He disliked academies, titles, and ceremonial occasions, feeling that those things had nothing to do with understanding things.

title: A Brooklyn accent
text: He spoke with a Queens, New York accent, never changed it his whole life, and had no intention of changing it.

title: Overturning himself
text: He often publicly overturned his own earlier ideas, holding that changing one's mind is not a disgrace but a normal part of doing things right.

title: Later years and death
text: In the 1980s he had liposarcoma and underwent several operations. He died in Los Angeles on February 15, 1988.
